input:
In this example, we are going to work through the calculation of the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent heat exchanger, which is a really important concept in heat transfer. The exchanger in question cools a process stream from 160 °C all the way down to 120 °C, using water that enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. In a countercurrent arrangement, the temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger are not the same, and here they work out to 85 K at the hot end and 80 K at the cold end. Because these differences are not equal, a simple arithmetic average is not strictly appropriate, and the log-mean temperature difference is used instead, since it properly reflects the way the driving force varies along the length of the exchanger. It is calculated using the well-known formula shown below:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

When the values of 85 K and 80 K are substituted into this formula, the log-mean temperature difference comes out to 82.5 K. It is worth noting that this result rests on certain assumptions, namely that the overall heat transfer coefficient remains constant along the exchanger and that no phase change takes place in either stream, so the value of 82.5 K should be applied with those conditions in mind.
target:
Calculate the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent exchanger that cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C. The temperature difference between the two streams is not constant along the exchanger, so the driving force for heat transfer is represented by a mean taken over the length. The terminal differences, formed from the temperatures at the two ends, are 85 K at the end where the process stream enters and 80 K at the end where it leaves. Where the two terminal differences differ, the mean is the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$, defined by

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

in which the symbols in the numerator and the denominator are the two terminal differences. Substitution of 85 K and 80 K gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 82.5 K. The check is the arithmetic mean of the same two differences, 82.5 K: the log mean lies close to the arithmetic mean because the terminal differences are close to each other, and it falls between them, as a mean must. The value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream; a stream that condenses or boils develops a different temperature profile and takes a different treatment.
